cards.front: A {{c1::resource}} is something a living thing needs, such as food, water, shelter, a mate or territory.
cards.quote: A resource is something a living thing needs, such as food, water, shelter, a mate or territory.
cards.section: Read the evidence: alone and together

cards.front: What is a community in biology?
cards.back: All the populations in an area that interact.
cards.quote: A community is all the populations in an area that interact.
cards.section: Read the evidence: alone and together

cards.front: What is territory?
cards.back: The area an animal uses and keeps others out of.
cards.quote: Territory is the area an animal uses and keeps others out of.
cards.section: Read the evidence: alone and together

cards.front: In Gause's paramecium tubes, he added a fresh, measured amount of food each day. Why is it important that the amount was measured?
cards.back: Gause added a fresh, measured amount each day, so the food supply was known and limited. Then changes in the counts could be linked to the food and to sharing the tube.
cards.why: A fair test keeps the food amount constant.
cards.quote: Every day, Gause added a fresh, measured amount of bacterial food to each tube and counted a measured sample.
cards.section: Read the evidence: alone and together

cards.front: In the paramecium model, you keep one kind alone and change its daily food from medium to low. How does its highest bar change, and does it grow forever?
cards.back: The highest bar is lower with low food. It does not grow forever in either run.
cards.why: Less food supports a lower population, and limited food stops growth.
cards.quote: The population grows in both runs, but less food supports a lower population.
cards.section: Explore: share a tube of food

cards.front: In Gause's tubes, what helped stop paramecium growth once the tube was crowded?
cards.back: Running out of food. The paramecia ate each day's bacteria until the liquid cleared. Gause also wrote that other conditions in the liquid mattered.
cards.quote: Running out of food helped stop their growth, though Gause wrote that other conditions in the liquid mattered too.
cards.section: Read the evidence: alone and together

cards.front: In Gause's 1934 counts on day 12, P. aurelia alone had 610 per 0.5 mL sample and P. caudatum alone had 199. About how many times as common was aurelia?
cards.back: 610 / 199 is about 3.1, so aurelia was about three times as common.
cards.quote: Divide 610 by 199. The result is about 3.1, so aurelia was about three times as common.
cards.section: Read the evidence: alone and together

cards.front: On day 25, P. caudatum had 180 per sample alone and 20 sharing. P. aurelia had 510 alone and 350 sharing. Which kind lost more per sample, and which lost the bigger share of its population?
cards.back: Both lost 160 per sample (180 - 20 and 510 - 350). Caudatum lost the bigger share: 20 is only about 11% of 180, while 350 is about 69% of 510.
cards.why: The drops are equal, but a drop of 160 matters more when the starting number is smaller.
cards.quote: Twenty is a small part of 180, while 350 is still a large part of 510.
cards.section: Read the evidence: alone and together

cards.front: In Gause's table, P. caudatum sharing a tube peaked on day 8. What happened after that, and did the population reach zero by day 25?
cards.back: It fell on every day shown, from 124 to 20 per sample by day 25. It had not reached zero.
cards.quote: After that it fell on every day shown, to 20 by day 25, but it had not reached zero.
cards.section: Read the evidence: alone and together

cards.front: In Gause's table, on days 4 and 6 both paramecium kinds were higher sharing a tube than alone. Does one early day like that show that sharing is helpful?
cards.back: No. Later counts showed both kinds ended lower sharing than alone. One early comparison cannot give the whole pattern, so read all the days.
cards.quote: On days 4 and 6, both kinds were higher together than alone.
cards.section: Read the evidence: alone and together

cards.front: Why do living things often compete without fighting?
cards.back: Competing means needing the same limited resource, and often that means getting it first, not fighting.
cards.quote: Key idea: Living things compete when they need the same limited resource, and often that means getting it first, not fighting.

cards.front: Name the three limited resources plants compete for, and tell one way a tall plant can win.
cards.back: Light, water and minerals. A tall plant can shade a short one.
cards.quote: Plants compete for light, water and minerals. A tall plant can shade a short one.

cards.front: Two plants grow close together in a garden. Which limited resource do they share above ground, and which two do their roots share below ground?
cards.back: They share light above ground. Their roots draw water and minerals from the same soil.
cards.quote: The plants share light above ground. Their roots draw water and minerals from the same soil below ground.

cards.front: Honeybees, wolves and schools of fish work together. Name the three kinds of needs cooperation can help members meet.
cards.back: Get food, stay safe and raise young.
cards.quote: Key idea: Working together can help members of a population get food, stay safe and raise young.

cards.front: Does cooperation make every member's share equal or remove the limits on a population?
cards.back: No. Working together does not make every share equal, and it does not remove limits.
cards.quote: Working together does not make every share equal, and it does not remove limits.

cards.front: A {{c1::limiting factor}} is anything in the environment that can restrict which species, or how many of a species, live in an ecosystem.
cards.quote: A limiting factor is anything in the environment that can restrict which species, or how many of a species, live in an ecosystem.

cards.front: Sort these limiting factors as biotic (living) or abiotic (nonliving): food, water, disease, predation, cold weather.
cards.back: Biotic: food, disease, predation. Abiotic: water, cold weather.
cards.quote: A hard freeze can kill many animals at once.

cards.front: Shelter can be biotic or abiotic. Give one example of each.
cards.back: A hollow tree is living (biotic) shelter. A gap in rocks is nonliving (abiotic) shelter.
cards.quote: A hollow tree is living shelter; a gap in rocks is nonliving shelter.

cards.front: A disease kills many rabbits in a forest. Name two ways this change spreads to other populations.
cards.back: Foxes that eat rabbits have less food, so fewer foxes may survive. The plants the rabbits ate will probably grow more, since fewer rabbits eat them.
cards.why: Linked populations affect each other along more than one link.
cards.quote: With fewer rabbits eating them, the plants will probably grow more.

cards.front: In a pond, a dry summer shrinks the water. Why is this an abiotic limiting factor, and what can happen to the frog population?
cards.back: Water is nonliving, so it is abiotic. In a dry summer, some animals and plants die, so fewer frogs may survive.
cards.quote: In a dry summer, some animals and plants die.

cards.front: A class plans a radish test of whether crowding makes plants compete. What should be the independent variable, the dependent variable and the control?
cards.back: Independent variable: plants per pot (such as 1, 4, 8 and 16). Dependent variable: mean mass of each plant in grams after three weeks. Control: pots with one plant, which have no neighbors to compete with.
cards.quote: Control: pots with one plant, which has no neighbors to compete with.

cards.front: In the radish test, mean mass per plant falls as plants per pot rise. What can you claim, and what must stay the same for the claim to be fair?
cards.back: The plants were probably competing for light, water or minerals. Pot size, soil, daily water in mL, light and temperature must be the same, with at least three pots per crowding level.
cards.why: Constants and repeated trials keep crowding as the only change.
cards.quote: What results would mean: if mean mass per plant falls as crowding rises, the plants were probably competing for light, water or minerals.

cards.front: Two paramecium kinds share one tube of food each day. One uses the same food as the other, and a second pair uses mostly different food. Which pair is more likely to stay common together, and why?
cards.back: The pair using different food. Less overlap means less competition for the same limited resource, so each kind is held back less.
cards.why: Rests on: competition happens when kinds need the same limited resource.
cards.quote: Record which setup lets both populations remain common.
cards.section: Explore: share a tube of food

cards.front: Wolves hunt in a pack. A lone wolf and a pack both need food. How could cooperation help the pack, and does it remove the limits on the pack?
cards.back: Working together can help members get food and stay safe, but it does not remove limits, so the wolves still face limits.
cards.why: Rests on: cooperation helps members meet needs but does not remove limits.
cards.quote: Working together does not make every share equal, and it does not remove limits.
